section.title: The Conversion of Saul
section.sectionRationale: The great persecutor becomes the great apostle. Saul, still breathing threats and armed with letters to arrest believers in Damascus, is stopped on the road by the risen Christ, who identifies Himself with the church Saul is hunting. Blinded and humbled, he is sent to a fearful Ananias, filled with the Spirit, baptized, and at once begins to preach that Jesus is the Son of God. This is the calling of the man who will carry the name of Christ to the Gentiles.
section.thesis: The risen Jesus sovereignly and graciously arrests His fiercest enemy, revealing that to persecute the church is to persecute Christ Himself, and turns Saul into a chosen instrument to carry His name to the nations, so that no one is beyond the reach of grace and no life is too far gone to be remade for mission.
section.frameNote: Five movements: Saul breathing threats on the way to Damascus; the light, the voice, and three days blind; Ananias sent to the chosen instrument; Saul preaching Christ boldly in Damascus and escaping the plot; and his wary reception in Jerusalem as the church finds peace.

units.label: Saul breathing threats
units.note: the persecutor sets out for Damascus

verses.text: Meanwhile, Saul was still breathing out murderous threats against the disciples of the Lord. He approached the high priest
and requested letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any men or women belonging to the {{hodos|Way}}, he could bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem.

units.label: The light on the road
units.note: Saul, why do you persecute Me

verses.text: As Saul drew near to Damascus on his journey, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him.
He fell to the ground and heard a voice say to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you {{dioko|persecute}} Me?”
“Who are You, Lord?” Saul asked. “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” He replied.
“Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.”
The men traveling with Saul stood there speechless. They heard the voice but did not see anyone.
Saul got up from the ground, but when he opened his eyes he could not see a thing. So they led him by the hand into Damascus.
For three days he was without sight, and he did not eat or drink anything.

units.label: Ananias and the chosen instrument
units.note: the Lord sends a fearful disciple to Saul

verses.text: In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias. The Lord spoke to him in a vision, “Ananias!” “Here I am, Lord,” he answered.
“Get up!” the Lord told him. “Go to the house of Judas on Straight Street and ask for a man from Tarsus named Saul, for he is praying.
In a vision he has seen a man named Ananias come and place his hands on him to restore his sight.”
But Ananias answered, “Lord, many people have told me about this man and all the harm he has done to Your saints in Jerusalem.
And now he is here with authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on Your name.”
“Go!” said the Lord. “This man is My chosen {{skeuos|instrument}} to carry My name before the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel.
I will show him how much he must suffer for My name.”

So Ananias went to the house, and when he arrived, he placed his hands on Saul. “Brother Saul,” he said, “the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here, has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”
At that instant, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and his sight was restored. He got up and was baptized,
and after taking some food, he regained his strength. And he spent several days with the disciples in Damascus.

units.label: Saul preaches at Damascus
units.note: proving that Jesus is the Christ

verses.text: Saul promptly began to proclaim Jesus in the synagogues, declaring, “He is the Son of God.”
All who heard him were astounded and asked, “Isn’t this the man who wreaked havoc in Jerusalem on those who call on this name? And hasn’t he come here to take them as prisoners to the chief priests?”
But Saul was empowered all the more, and he confounded the Jews living in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the {{christos|Christ}}.
After many days had passed, the Jews conspired to kill him,
but Saul learned of their plot. Day and night they watched the city gates in order to kill him.
One night, however, his disciples took him and lowered him in a basket through a window in the wall.

units.label: Saul in Jerusalem and the church at peace
units.note: Barnabas vouches for him, and the church is strengthened

verses.text: When Saul arrived in Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.
Then Barnabas brought him to the apostles and described how Saul had seen the Lord, who had spoken to him on the road to Damascus, and how Saul had spoken boldly in that city in the name of Jesus.
So Saul stayed with them, moving about freely in Jerusalem and speaking boldly in the name of the Lord.
He talked and debated with the Grecian Jews, but they tried to kill him.
When the brothers learned of this, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
Then the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria experienced a time of peace. It grew in strength and numbers, living in the fear of the Lord and the encouragement of the Holy Spirit.

hodos.gloss: A road or way. In Acts the Way becomes an early name for the Christian movement, those who follow Jesus who called Himself the way. It is fitting that Saul, hunting followers of the Way, is stopped on a literal road and set on a new path.

dioko.gloss: To pursue, to persecute. The risen Christ asks why Saul persecutes Me, not merely My people, revealing that the Lord is so united to His church that to attack them is to attack Him. This union grounds Paul's later theology of the body of Christ.

skeuos.gloss: A vessel or instrument. Christ calls Saul a chosen vessel to carry His name to the nations. The word underlines grace: Saul is not chosen for his worthiness but taken up and put to use by the Lord who saved him.

christos.gloss: The Anointed One, the Messiah. Saul's whole mission is summed up in proving that Jesus is the Christ, the promised King of Israel, crucified and risen, the same claim that had made him a persecutor now becomes the message he preaches.

basic.context: Saul has been introduced as a violent enemy of the church, and here he is still breathing threats, heading to Damascus with legal papers to arrest believers. On the road the risen Jesus appears in blazing light and asks why Saul is persecuting Him, identifying Himself with His people. Blinded, Saul is led into the city, and God sends a frightened disciple named Ananias to heal and baptize him. At once Saul starts preaching that Jesus is the Son of God. The key questions are: what does it mean that Christ says you are persecuting Me, why is Saul chosen, and how does the church come to trust him?
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as a true conversion and a true commissioning at once. The turning point is not Saul's search for God but God's seizing of Saul, so the chapter magnifies sovereign grace. Christ's words in verse 4 are the theological heart: the union of Christ and His church. The rest describes how a real conversion works out in baptism, bold witness, suffering, and slow acceptance by the wider church.
basic.originalLanguages: Saul is hunting those who belong to the Way, the hodos, when the Lord asks why he persecutes, dioko, Him. Jesus names Saul a chosen instrument, skeuos, a vessel taken up for His purposes. And Saul's message becomes the proof that Jesus is the Christos, the Messiah. The words move from persecution to mission in a few strokes.
basic.typology: The scales falling from Saul's eyes picture the spiritual blindness that only Christ can lift. His three days without sight, food, or drink, followed by new life, echo a death and resurrection pattern. Ananias, an unremarkable disciple used for a great purpose, shows how God works through ordinary servants.
basic.christ: The whole account turns on the risen Christ. He appears alive, He speaks, He claims to be one with His suffering people, and He commissions Saul. From that moment Saul preaches Christ as the Son of God and proves He is the Messiah. The conversion is not to a philosophy but to a living Lord who confronts, forgives, and sends.
basic.god: God is sovereign and gracious. He stops His enemy in his tracks, chooses him for service before Saul has done a thing to earn it, overrules the fears of Ananias, and protects Saul from plots. He also warns that Saul must suffer for the name, showing that grace and hardship travel together in God's service.
basic.crossReferences: Galatians 1 gives Paul's own account of this call by grace. 1 Timothy 1 calls him the foremost of sinners shown mercy. 1 Corinthians 15 lists the risen Christ appearing to him last of all. Acts 26 retells the road to Damascus before Agrippa.
basic.oneStory: The chief enemy of the gospel becomes its chief herald. In one conversion God shows that no rebel is beyond His reach, and He raises up the apostle who will carry the name of Jesus across the empire to the Gentiles, driving the story of Acts toward the ends of the earth.

context.literary:
Luke tells this story three times, here in the third person and later in Paul's own voice, Acts 22 and Acts 26, and the repetition tells us how much weight he gives it. The first telling is the narrator's account, and it is built as a reversal in four panels. Saul sets out as the hunter with letters, 9:1-2. He is stopped, struck blind and led by the hand, 9:3-9. He is met by a hesitant disciple who calls him 'Brother Saul,' 9:10-19. And he is then hunted himself, first in Damascus and then in Jerusalem, 9:23-30. The man who came to drag others in chains has to be led, and the man who threatened to kill has to be let down a wall in a basket.

The reversals are marked by echoes of the opening verse. Saul went to Damascus to bring believers as prisoners, 9:2; Ananias will take his hand and lead him, 9:8, 9:17. Saul came with authority from the chief priests, 9:14; he leaves with a commission from Christ, 9:15. Saul was breathing threats and murder; in 9:22 he is 'empowered all the more' to prove who Jesus is. The people who are astonished in 9:21 recite his old reputation exactly as the first verse had drawn it.

The central scene is a dialogue within a dialogue. The Lord speaks to Saul, and then the Lord speaks to Ananias, and in the second conversation the Lord does something unusual: He lets a disciple object. Ananias has four sentences of protest, 9:13-14, and receives a single command, 'Go!', followed by the reason, 9:15-16. The Lord answers a servant's fear without rebuking it.

The unit closes with the summary of 9:31, the first of Luke's progress notes since Acts 6:7. The church now has peace, grows, and is 'built up.' It comes straight after Saul has been sent away to Tarsus, and the placement is not an accident. With the chief persecutor gone from the scene, the church can breathe.
context.historical:
Damascus was a major city north-east of Judea with a large Jewish population and many synagogues. Saul's request for letters to those synagogues shows how far the high priest's influence was thought to reach among Jews of the diaspora. Whatever the exact legal arrangements, Luke's point is that Saul meant to carry the persecution out of Jerusalem and into the places where the scattered believers had fled, Acts 8:1-4.

Paul gives his own background in several places. He was a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, and as to zeal a persecutor of the church, Philippians 3:5-6. He was advancing in Judaism beyond many of his contemporaries and was extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers, Galatians 1:13-14. His Tarsus home lay in Cilicia, and Cilicians had been among those who argued with Stephen, Acts 6:9. When Saul begins to debate with the Grecian Jews in Jerusalem in 9:29, he is arguing with the same circle that had opposed Stephen, and they try to kill him as they killed Stephen.

Paul's letters fill in the timeline Luke compresses. After his conversion he went into Arabia and returned to Damascus, and only after three years did he go up to Jerusalem to meet Cephas, Galatians 1:17-18. The 'many days' of Acts 9:23 therefore cover a long season, not a few weeks. Paul also remembers the escape from Damascus, where the governor under King Aretas had the city watched and he was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall, 2 Corinthians 11:32-33. Aretas was the Nabatean king, which shows how far the opposition to Saul in Damascus extended beyond the synagogue.

Barnabas, who introduces Saul to the apostles, was a Levite from Cyprus whose name means Son of Encouragement, Acts 4:36. He is the right man for the work, since the Jerusalem church had every reason to fear that Saul's conversion was a trap. The church's caution in 9:26 is not unbelief but memory.
context.canonical:
The Damascus road is the centre of Paul's own story and he returns to it again and again. He tells the Galatians that God set him apart from his mother's womb and was pleased to reveal His Son in him, Galatians 1:15-16. He lists himself last among those to whom the risen Christ appeared, as one untimely born, 1 Corinthians 15:8-10, and he sets his own mercy as a pattern, 'so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience,' 1 Timothy 1:16. Acts itself retells the road to the people of Jerusalem, Acts 22, and to Agrippa, Acts 26, and each time the details are shaped by the audience.

The scene belongs to a line of Old Testament calls. The doubled name, 'Saul, Saul,' echoes 'Abraham, Abraham,' Genesis 22:11, 'Moses, Moses,' Exodus 3:4, and 'Samuel! Samuel!' 1 Samuel 3:10, and Acts 26:14 notes that the voice spoke in Hebrew. Paul's own words about being set apart from the womb recall Jeremiah 1:5 and Isaiah 49:1-6, and in Acts 13:47 he applies Isaiah 49:6, the Servant as a light for the nations, to his own mission. The company's terror in Daniel 10:7, where only the prophet sees the vision, throws light on the travellers who heard but did not see.

Christ's identification with His people is taught elsewhere. 'Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me,' Matthew 25:40, and 'If they persecuted Me, they will persecute you as well,' John 15:20. Behind both stands the word of Zechariah 2:8, that whoever touches God's people touches the apple of His eye. Paul will later turn the same truth into his doctrine of the church as the body of Christ, 1 Corinthians 12:12, and the root of that doctrine is a single question on a road.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke writes for a church that was still afraid of Saul, and for later churches who would meet people they could not imagine being saved. The chapter is meant to settle two questions at once. How could the greatest enemy of the church become its greatest apostle? And on what authority did Paul preach? Luke's answer to the first is that Christ did it Himself, in power and without any help from Saul, and to the second that Paul's commission came directly from the risen Lord and was then confirmed by the church, by Ananias in Damascus and Barnabas in Jerusalem.

The details are tied together so that the reader cannot separate the call from the community. Saul is not left alone with his vision. He is sent to a disciple, healed by a disciple's hands, baptized, fed and kept by the Damascus disciples, and vouched for by Barnabas. The Lord who confronts him alone also puts him straight into the body.

Luke also means to prepare the reader for suffering. The Lord's words in 9:16 tell the reader what to expect in the rest of the book: a ministry that is bold and costly together. The grace that saves Saul does not excuse him from the cross, and the apostles' own fear of him is turned, over the course of the book, into love.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The narrative records one man's conversion. It does not require every conversion to look like it. Few believers meet the risen Christ in a blinding light, hear His voice, and are struck blind for three days. Luke does not present the lightning as the model but as the means of a particular commissioning. What is normative is what is common to Saul's story and every other: the Lord takes the initiative, the sinner is humbled, a fellow believer ministers to him, baptism follows, and the new believer confesses Christ.

The words of the Lord about persecution are description of Saul's own calling, not a promise that every follower will suffer in the same degree, though Jesus does say that those who follow Him will meet opposition, John 15:20. The church's response is more directly instructive. Ananias obeys even when he is afraid, and Barnabas takes a risk on a man the others do not trust. Both are held up as models of the faith that acts on the Lord's word against its own fears.

Luke also does not teach that a believer should wait for supernatural direction before welcoming a new convert. The Lord's word to Ananias is specific to his situation; the principle that carries over is that a church should not let its past hurt decide whom grace may reach.

debates.question: Was this a conversion or a call?

views.label: A conversion from one religion to another
views.case: Saul himself says he counted his old life as loss, Philippians 3:7-9, and describes it as his 'former way of life in Judaism,' Galatians 1:13. He was baptized, called on the name of Jesus, and was turned from darkness to light, Acts 22:16 and 26:18. Whatever he kept from his heritage, he was a new creation in Christ, and the church of Damascus received him as a convert.

views.label: A call within Israel to a new mission
views.case: Some modern readers stress that Paul never speaks of leaving the God of Israel and that the language of Galatians 1:15-16 is the language of the call of a prophet, Jeremiah 1:5. He is set apart and sent to the nations. On this view the road is mainly a commissioning, and the word 'conversion' suggests a break with his people that Paul himself would not have described that way.

views.label: Both a conversion and a call
views.case: Luke gives both in a single sequence: the Lord confronts him, he is humbled, he is baptized and filled with the Spirit, and at once he is told he is a chosen instrument. Paul's own account pairs the forgiven persecutor of 1 Timothy 1:13-16 with the appointed servant of 1 Timothy 1:12. The two belong together.

debates.bearing: The text supports both emphases, and the third reading respects the language of repentance and the language of commission without reducing either. How the question is answered shapes how Paul's continuing relation to Israel is read.

debates.question: What do the companions hear and see?

views.label: The accounts can be harmonised by what is meant by hearing
views.case: Acts 9:7 says the men 'heard the voice but did not see anyone,' while Acts 22:9 says they 'saw the light, but they could not understand the voice.' The first can mean they heard the sound, and the second that they did not make out the words, since the Greek verb 'to hear' can carry either sense. Some have argued from the difference in grammatical case, but that distinction is not consistent enough in Greek to carry the weight alone.

views.label: Luke's retellings emphasise different aspects for different audiences
views.case: The three accounts differ in detail: who fell, who stood, which words were spoken at which point, and how much of the commission is given to Saul directly or through Ananias. Luke, who is a careful writer, does not hide the differences, which suggests he is more interested in the main facts than in reproducing every word in the same form.

debates.bearing: Neither view threatens the central claims: a real light, a real voice, a real Jesus. Readers who hold to the full truthfulness of Scripture will resist forced harmonies and will not mind that eyewitnesses differ on what they perceived.

study.originalLanguages:
Luke's opening describes Saul as empneon apeiles kai phonou, literally breathing in threat and murder. The verb is the one used of respiration, as though threat and slaughter were the air he lived on. It is a picture of a man for whom persecution has become second nature, and the Lord's work on the road is to change what he breathes.

The Lord's first word is 'Saul, Saul,' and here the Greek keeps the Hebrew form of the name, Saoul, rather than the Greek Saulos that Luke will use later. Acts 26:14 says the voice spoke in Hebrew. The doubled call is the call of a God who knows a person by name, as in Genesis 22:11 and Exodus 3:4. And Saul's question, 'Who are You, Lord?' uses kyrie, a word that may mean 'sir' on his lips and 'Lord' on the lips of the Lord's people. In the answer the word fills with its full meaning.

When the Lord tells Ananias about Saul, He says he is a skeuos ekloges, a vessel of choice, 9:15. The phrase is a favourite of Paul's own, who writes of vessels of mercy prepared in advance, Romans 9:23, and who carries a treasure in jars of clay, 2 Corinthians 4:7. The task is to bastazo, to carry, the name before the nations, the verb for bearing a burden. The weight of the name is borne by the man who once set out to erase it. And the Lord says Saul 'must' suffer, dei, the word of divine necessity that Luke uses of the cross itself, Luke 24:26. The same dei governs the suffering of Christ and of His chosen vessel.

The word 'name' is repeated through the chapter like a beat: those who call on Your name, 9:14; carry My name, 9:15; suffer for My name, 9:16; those who call on this name, 9:21; and he spoke boldly in the name of Jesus, 9:27 and 9:28. The verb for calling on the name, epikaleo, is the verb of Joel 2:32, quoted at Pentecost, Acts 2:21, and the mark of believers in 9:14 and 9:21. The persecutor hunted those who called on the name and ends up calling on it himself, 22:16.

The description of the healing uses an unusual word. Something like scales, lepides, fell from his eyes, 9:18. The word is found nowhere else in the New Testament, and the 'something like' keeps the language modest, a careful, modest way of describing what looked like flakes falling away.

In 9:22 Saul 'proves' that Jesus is the Christ with the verb sumbibazo, which means to bring together, to join one thing to another, and so to conclude. He puts Scriptures and events side by side until the conclusion follows. And he spoke 'boldly,' parrhesiazomai, 9:27 and 9:28, the verb of open, unashamed speech, which belongs to Acts from Peter and John in chapter 4 onward.

The last verse says the church was 'built up,' oikodomeo, and lived in the 'encouragement,' paraklesis, of the Holy Spirit. It is the root behind the name Barnabas, Son of Encouragement, Acts 4:36, the man who has just brought Saul in.

typology.type: The light that opens the blind, Isaiah 42:6-7 and Acts 9:3, 9:18
typology.fulfillment: The Servant of Isaiah 42 is given 'to open the eyes of the blind' and to be a light to the nations, 42:6-7. Saul is struck by a light from heaven and loses his sight, and when Ananias lays hands on him he sees again. Paul himself reads the event as new creation: the God who said 'Let light shine out of darkness' made His light shine in his heart, 2 Corinthians 4:6. The escalation is that the light is the face of Christ, and the commission that follows is to open the eyes of others, Acts 26:18. The type falls short only in that Saul's blindness is a sign, and the real blindness the Lord heals is of the heart.

typology.type: Three days and a baptism, Acts 9:9 and 9:18
typology.fulfillment: Saul spends three days without sight, food or drink, and then rises and is baptized. Luke does not draw the link himself, so the correspondence is to be held lightly. Jesus spoke of three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, Matthew 12:40, and Paul later teaches that baptism is burial with Christ and rising to walk in newness of life, Romans 6:3-4. The pattern is that the old man goes down into helplessness and the new man comes up in Christ. It falls short of a one-to-one picture, because Saul's three days are a period of humbling and prayer, not a re-enactment.

typology.type: Rescued through a window, Joshua 2:15, 1 Samuel 19:12 and Acts 9:25
typology.fulfillment: Rahab lowered the spies through a window in the city wall, Joshua 2:15, and Michal lowered David from a window when Saul sent men to kill him, 1 Samuel 19:11-12. When the Jews of Damascus watch the gates, Saul's disciples lower him in a basket through the wall, and Paul remembers it, 2 Corinthians 11:32-33. The pattern is that of the hunted servant whom God preserves, and the irony is sharp: the man who bears the name of the first king Saul is now in David's position, hunted by Israel's leaders. The correspondence is a literary echo and not a prophecy, but it teaches that God preserves His chosen for His purpose.

typology.type: The appointed servant set apart from the womb, Jeremiah 1:5 and Galatians 1:15
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah was set apart before birth and appointed a prophet to the nations, Jeremiah 1:5, and the Servant of Isaiah 49 is called from the womb to be a light for the nations. Paul uses the same language of himself in Galatians 1:15-16 and applies Isaiah 49:6 to his work in Acts 13:47. In the end Christ is the true Servant who is the light, and Paul is His herald. The escalation is that the mission to the nations, which in Jeremiah was a task of judgment and warning, is now the carrying of the name of Christ to the Gentiles. The type falls short in that the prophets suffered in order to speak God's word, while Christ suffers to accomplish what the word promised.

study.christ:
The whole chapter turns on a person. The Lord asks, 'Why do you persecute Me?' and when Saul asks who He is, the answer is not an argument but a name: 'I am Jesus.' The risen Christ is not a memory or an idea. He is a living Lord who speaks from heaven, who knows the street and the house in Damascus where Saul is staying, who knows that Saul is praying, and who has already shown Saul a vision of Ananias coming to restore his sight, 9:11-12.

His identification with His people is complete. The persecution was against disciples, yet He says 'Me.' Matthew 25:40 teaches that service to the least of His brothers is service to Him, and John 15:20 teaches that persecution of the servant is persecution of the Master. On the road the doctrine is made flesh. It is also the seed of Paul's later teaching that the church is the body of Christ, 1 Corinthians 12:12.

Saul's first sermon sets out who Jesus is: 'He is the Son of God,' 9:20, and then that He is the Christ, 9:22. The first title speaks of His identity, the second of His office. Saul does not argue from his experience alone but proves it from the Scriptures, putting passage beside passage, and the Son of God is shown to be the Messiah that the Law and the prophets promised.

The Lord also commissions in His own authority. He appoints Saul to carry His name to Gentiles, kings and Israel, 9:15, and in Acts 26:16-18 He says that He has appeared to him as a servant and witness. That is the footing of Paul's claim to be an apostle, 1 Corinthians 9:1 and 15:8. The Lord who gave the first apostles their mission, Acts 1:8, gives Saul his, from heaven.

Finally the Lord shows what the mission will cost. 'I will show him how much he must suffer for My name,' 9:16. Christ Himself had said the Son of Man must suffer, Luke 9:22, and now His servant will share what He shared. In 1 Timothy 1:16 Paul says that Christ displayed His perfect patience in him as an example. The patience of the Lord who endured the cross is the same patience that endured the persecutor.

A caution: not everything in the account is a code for Christ. The blindness, the basket and the street are historical details, and the account is not served by making each a symbol. The links that matter are those the text and the apostle himself draw: the Lord's identification with His church, His authority to commission, and His grace to the worst of sinners.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is sovereign in a way that is almost frightening. He stops a man who has not asked to be stopped. Saul does not seek God on the road, he is not repenting, and he has not had a change of heart. The change begins entirely on God's side, with a light and a voice. Paul never forgets this: 'by the grace of God I am what I am,' 1 Corinthians 15:10, and he says God was 'pleased' to reveal His Son in him, Galatians 1:15-16. The language of pleasure belongs to a God who acts freely.

He is also astonishingly personal. He speaks Saul's name twice, He knows the street and the house and the name of the host in Damascus, and He knows that Saul is praying, 9:11. He gives Saul a vision of Ananias before Ananias arrives. A God who is this attentive to the details of one man's life is not the God of a distant plan but the God who numbers the hairs of the head.

He is patient with His people's fears. Ananias raises the very objection the church would have raised, and the Lord does not rebuke him. He explains. The Lord who has authority to order a prophet to go is also gentle enough to listen to an anxious disciple, and the result is a servant who calls his enemy 'Brother Saul.'

He is just and merciful together. Saul is struck blind, a sign that the persecutor is under judgment, and healed, a sign that he is forgiven. He is told he will suffer. Grace does not remove the cost; it gives the cost a meaning. Paul says that he was shown mercy because he had acted in ignorance and unbelief, 1 Timothy 1:13, and that the Lord made him an example of patience.

He is faithful to His church. The final verse shows peace, growth and encouragement. God does not abandon His people when the persecutor is converted or when the persecutor remains. The church lives in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Spirit, and the same God who stopped the hunter protects the hunted.

For worship the chapter asks us to pray for our enemies with real expectation. No one is too far gone. The God who found Saul on the road to Damascus can find anyone on any road.

crossReferences.note: Paul's own account says he persecuted the church severely, was set apart from his mother's womb and called by grace, and that God was pleased to reveal His Son in him. He adds that he went into Arabia and returned to Damascus, a detail Luke leaves out.

Paul calls himself a former blasphemer, persecutor and violent man who was shown mercy, and says Christ displayed His perfect patience in him as an example for later believers. His conversion is offered as a pattern for everyone who is tempted to think himself beyond grace.

Paul lists himself last among those to whom the risen Christ appeared and calls himself 'one of untimely birth.' He bases his apostleship on that appearance and gives the credit to the grace of God, and not to himself.

Paul counts up his credentials, circumcised, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, a persecutor, faultless in the law, and says he counts them loss for the sake of Christ. The list shows what Saul was on the road in Acts 9 and what he gave up.

Paul retells the road before Agrippa and adds the words 'It is hard for you to kick against the goads,' and a commission to open eyes from darkness to light. It shows how the same events are reported to a different audience.

In this telling the companions saw the light but could not understand the voice. Set beside Acts 9:7, the two verses invite a careful reading of what the companions perceived and show that Luke saw no need to remove the apparent tension.

The King says that whatever was done for the least of His brothers was done for Him. The Lord's question on the road, 'Why do you persecute Me?', applies the same principle in the negative: harm to His people is harm to Him.
The LORD says that whoever touches His people touches the apple of His eye. The Old Testament already taught the union between God and His people that Christ states on the Damascus road.

The Servant is made a light for the nations, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth. Paul quotes it of his own mission in Acts 13:47, which shows that he understood his call as sharing in the Servant's work.
Paul's own memory of the escape from Damascus, lowered in a basket through a window in the wall, confirms Luke's account independently and adds that the governor under King Aretas was involved.

Barnabas, the Son of Encouragement, is the one who vouches for Saul in 9:27. The matching word for encouragement appears in 9:31 for the Spirit's work among the churches, so that the man and the Spirit's gift share the same root.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is a story of a God who goes after those who run from Him. He calls to Adam in the garden, 'Where are you?' He meets Jacob at night and Moses in a bush, and He stops the prophet Jonah in a storm. The conversion of Saul is the same pursuit in the new age, directed at the man most set against the new thing God was doing.

It also answers the question the story has been asking since Genesis 3: can the enemy of God's people be reconciled? Cain killed Abel, the nations raged against Israel, and the leaders of Jerusalem killed the Son. Now one of the angriest of them is overcome by grace. Paul says that this is the pattern: where sin increased, grace increased all the more, Romans 5:20. The Pharisee who thought he was serving God discovers that he has been fighting Him, and the discovery makes him the man who writes most of the New Testament's letters.

The conversion is also the hinge of Acts. Since Acts 1:8 the mission has moved from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria, and the next step is the ends of the earth. Luke has shown the first martyr; now the man who watched him die becomes the missionary. The Lord says that Saul will carry His name to the Gentiles and their kings, as well as to Israel, 9:15. The promise to Abraham that all the nations would be blessed, Genesis 12:3, now has a messenger who will cross the Mediterranean to deliver it.

And the chapter looks ahead to the end. The vision of the multitude from every nation in Revelation 7:9 includes people whose first reaction to the gospel was hatred. A church that has been shown that its worst enemy can be its brother will never again treat any person as beyond the reach of the Lord who found Saul.

sermon.title: One Changed Life (Acts 9:1-18)
sermon.why: Begg preaches Saul's conversion as the work of God's sovereign, gradual, gentle grace, showing that the same grace that seized the church's fiercest enemy is what frees and remakes any sinner, which is precisely the heart of this study.

quiz.q: What did the risen Jesus reveal by asking, why do you persecute Me?

options.text: That He is so united to His church that attacking His people is attacking Him.
options.note: Christ identifies Himself with the disciples Saul is hunting, the union of head and body.

options.text: That Saul had personally harmed Jesus during His earthly ministry.
options.note: Saul had persecuted the church, not the earthly Jesus; the point is Christ's union with His people now.

options.text: That Saul's opposition mattered to God because the disciples were suffering.
options.note: True that their suffering mattered, but the striking claim is that Christ counts it as done to Himself.

options.text: That Jesus was merely a memory the disciples clung to.
options.note: The living Christ speaks in person, disproving any idea that He was only a memory.

quiz.q: Why did the Lord choose Saul, according to the passage?

options.text: As a chosen instrument to carry Christ's name to the Gentiles, their kings, and Israel.
options.note: The Lord states this purpose to Ananias in verse 15.

options.text: Because Saul was a learned and zealous man whose gifts God could use.
options.note: His gifts were later used, but the text grounds the choice in God's purpose and grace, not Saul's worthiness.

options.text: To make him a witness who would also suffer much for the name.
options.note: True and stated in verse 16, but this is the cost attached to the mission, not the mission's main aim.

options.text: Because Saul had begun to soften and seek Christ on his own.
options.note: Saul was breathing threats, not seeking Christ; the initiative was entirely the Lord's.

quiz.q: How is the Damascus road event best understood?

options.text: As a genuine conversion and an apostolic commissioning at the same time.
options.note: Saul is truly saved and truly sent, both together, as Luke and Paul's letters show.

options.text: As mainly the prophetic call of an already devout worshipper of God.
options.note: This underplays Paul's own testimony that he was a persecutor shown mercy and made new.

options.text: As a conversion whose missionary calling unfolded over the years that followed.
options.note: Partly right, since the mission did unfold over time, but the commission was given at the outset, not only later.

options.text: As a vision with no lasting effect on Saul's life or beliefs.
options.note: The effect was total and permanent; the persecutor became the preacher at once.

quiz.q: Why were the Jerusalem disciples slow to accept Saul?

options.text: They were afraid of him and did not believe he was really a disciple.
options.note: Verse 26 states their fear and disbelief, until Barnabas vouched for him.

options.text: They were unsure whether his preaching in Damascus had been genuine.
options.note: Reasonable, and Barnabas addressed it by testifying to his bold witness, but the text names their fear that he was not a disciple at all.

options.text: They thought he needed more training before joining them.
options.note: The issue was trust and fear, not a lack of training.

options.text: They had never heard of Saul or his reputation.
options.note: They knew his reputation well, which is exactly why they were afraid.

quiz.q: What does Ananias's role teach about how God works?

options.text: God uses ordinary, even fearful, disciples to accomplish His great purposes.
options.note: Ananias is an unknown believer sent on a daunting errand, and God works powerfully through him.

options.text: God only entrusts important tasks to well-known leaders.
options.note: The opposite is shown; a little-known disciple is the one sent to the future apostle.

options.text: God expects His servants to obey even when they are afraid or reluctant.
options.note: True and important, but the fuller lesson is that God delights to use ordinary servants, not only that they must obey.

options.text: God rewards Ananias for volunteering eagerly for the task.
options.note: Ananias did not volunteer eagerly; he objected first, then obeyed the Lord's command.

questions: Christ told Saul that persecuting the church was persecuting Him. How does knowing that Jesus takes His people's suffering personally shape the way you treat other believers?
Saul was chosen while he was still an enemy, before he had done anything to deserve it. Where do you need to hear that grace comes to you as a gift and not a wage?
Ananias was afraid, yet he obeyed and went to Saul. Is there a hard step of obedience you have been avoiding because of fear of a particular person?
The Lord said Saul must suffer for the name. How does it steady you to know that following Christ can include real cost, not only comfort?
Barnabas took a risk to welcome a former enemy into the church. Who might God be calling you to receive or believe the best about, when others are still wary?

translationNotes.note: The BSB ends Jesus' reply at, I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. A footnote records that the later Textus Receptus adds, It is hard for you to kick against the goads, words that appear in Paul's own account in Acts 26:14; the BSB keeps them where the manuscripts best attest them.

The men heard the voice but saw no one. Paul's later retelling in Acts 22:9 says his companions did not understand the voice; the two accounts are reconciled by noting that they heard a sound without grasping its meaning.
The Grecian Jews, or Hellenists, were Greek-speaking Jews, the same group from which Stephen's opponents had come; Saul now debates the very circle he once served.
